title: Behavioral Health Scenario 12 (draft) – Inpatient Psychiatric Suicide Screening, Assessment, Safety Planning, Treatment, and Discharge
narrative:
Scenario 12.1 – Patient Narrative
Daniel, a 41-year-old, is admitted to an inpatient psychiatric unit after an emergency department evaluation following an intentional medication overdose. Patients reach the unit three ways: from an emergency department (the hospital's own or another), by transfer from another unit, or from the community through the hospital's admissions department, where a level-of-care assessment decides whether the patient needs inpatient care, partial hospitalization, or outpatient care.

On admission the hospital requests the outside record, including the ED record, and a master's-prepared clinician administers a suicide risk screener to every patient. A positive screen leads to a full suicide risk assessment (e.g., the C-SSRS, or an AMSR-based formulation); a negative screen does not. Daniel screens positive and is assessed as high risk, so nursing reassesses his suicide risk every shift for the length of his stay, physicians ask about risk as well, and the unit's universal precautions apply: belongings searched, his own medications secured, a ligature-resistant environment, and 15-minute checks.

Safety planning starts on admission, beginning with lethal means: what Daniel could reach at home, given his plan. Over the stay he identifies his triggers and protective factors, which become part of the intake or psychosocial assessment. Every day he attends active treatment - a morning check-in group where he sets a goal for the day, mindfulness, activity therapy, and DBT skills groups - and he completes symptom measures at admission and again at discharge.

At discharge every patient receives a suicide risk assessment. The physician, nurse and social worker assemble a multi-page set of discharge instructions, one page of which is Daniel's crisis safety plan; they review the plan with him against what he told them during the stay, revise it, and Daniel, each discipline and - with his agreement - his partner sign it. Before he goes home, someone other than Daniel confirms that firearms and stockpiled medications are secured, and his discharge prescriptions are limited in quantity. Because Daniel has an outpatient psychiatrist, the team confirms his follow-up appointment and hands him back; a patient without one is given an appointment with a new program. A next-day phone call would be best practice, but it is not built into the workflow.

The same steps apply to a patient admitted primarily for another reason - for example, psychosis - who also screens positive. What changes is the intensity: how often suicide risk is reassessed during the stay.
textPolicy: Source text is normalized ASCII punctuation, as in ed-scenario-11.json: straight quotes, hyphen-minus. En dashes in headings and the column names are kept to match the working group's format.
sourcePolicy: Each step's `transcript` field gives the timestamp range of the SME walkthrough (2026-05-29) it is drawn from. The transcript is not committed: it names people and an organization, and this document, like ed-scenario-11, names no real site, person, or vendor. A step with no transcript range is a SPiER proposal and carries `origin` and `rationale` instead.

sections.heading: Scenario 12.2 – Entry and Level of Care
sections.narrative: Patients enter inpatient psychiatric care from an emergency department (the hospital's own or another), by transfer from another unit, or from the community. A community patient - a walk-in, or one a community provider calls about - is sent to the hospital's admissions department for a level-of-care assessment rather than admitted directly. On admission the hospital requests the outside medical record, including the ED record.

sections.heading: Scenario 12.3 – Admission Screening and Assessment
sections.narrative: Every admitted patient is screened for suicide risk by a master's-prepared clinician, whatever the reason for admission. A positive screen leads to a full suicide risk assessment; a negative screen does not, and no lifetime assessment is done for a patient who did not screen positive. The resulting risk level sets how intensively risk is reassessed during the stay.
sections.summary: **Admission screening and assessment** - a universal screen, a full assessment on a positive result, and a risk level that sets reassessment intensity.

steps.inputs: Validated suicide risk screener (e.g., the C-SSRS screen); patient identity; encounter context

steps.actions: The admitting clinician screens every patient as part of the intake assessment, regardless of the reason for admission

sections.heading: Scenario 12.4 – During the Stay: Precautions and Reassessment
sections.narrative: Inpatient units take a universal-precautions stance: environments are ligature resistant, belongings are searched, patients' own medications are secured, and patients are checked every 15 minutes. On top of that, nursing reassesses suicide risk every shift for high-risk patients, and physicians ask about risk too. Stays are typically three to nine days, so repeated questioning is not a burden; a patient's denial is documented as an answer.
sections.summary: **During the stay** - universal precautions, per-shift nursing reassessment for high-risk patients, and physician risk evaluation.

steps.actions: Staff search belongings, secure or return the patient's own medications, run admission lab testing, and record 15-minute checks for the length of the stay

sections.heading: Scenario 12.5 – Safety Planning from Admission
sections.narrative: Safety planning starts on admission, not at discharge, and it starts with lethal means. Because the unit itself is secured, lethal-means work is about the patient's environment after discharge: whatever the patient's plan involves, the team works to make sure it is not accessible at home. Over the stay the patient identifies triggers and protective factors, which become part of the intake or psychosocial assessment.

sections.heading: Scenario 12.6 – Active Treatment and Measurement
sections.narrative: Every day, morning through night, patients attend active treatment: goal-setting and check-in groups, activity and music therapy, psychotherapy including CBT, DBT skills, and suicide-specific interventions. Symptom measures are taken at admission and at discharge. Today, which interventions a patient actually received is rarely available as structured data, so a facility cannot report how often an intervention is delivered or relate it to outcomes such as readmission - the gap the SME named as the one report they most want.
sections.summary: **Active treatment and measurement** - daily interventions captured as structured data, symptom measures at admission and discharge, and reporting across facilities.
sections.note: **This section holds the walkthrough's central gap.** The SME's most-wanted report was which interventions were actually delivered as a result of screening and assessment, comparable across facilities. That requires 12.6-1B to exist first.

sections.heading: Scenario 12.7 – Discharge
sections.narrative: Every patient receives a suicide risk assessment at discharge, whatever they were admitted for. The physician, nurse and social worker together produce the patient's discharge instructions, one page of which is the crisis safety plan. The team reviews the plan with the patient against what the patient said during the stay, revises it, and every discipline, the patient and - where possible - family sign it, on paper or electronically. Before a patient goes home, someone other than the patient confirms that the means identified in 12.5-1B are secured, and discharge prescriptions are limited in quantity.
sections.summary: **Discharge** - a universal discharge risk assessment, a co-signed safety plan, third-party confirmation of means safety, and limited discharge prescriptions.

sections.heading: Scenario 12.8 – Transition and Follow-Up
sections.narrative: As part of discharge planning, the team confirms a follow-up appointment. A patient who came from a provider goes back to that provider, with a handoff; a patient going to a new program is given an appointment with it, and education on how to get there. Post-discharge phone calls and caring contacts are considered important but are not built into the workflow, largely for lack of funded staff.
